title: Happy Number
summary: Develop an algorithm to check if a given positive integer n is a happy number.
statement: Develop an algorithm to check if a given positive integer n is a happy number. A happy number is defined by repeatedly replacing the number with the sum of the squares of its digits until it equals 1 or enters a cycle not including 1. Return true if n is happy, otherwise false.
constraints: Repeatedly replace n by the sum of the squares of its decimal digits. Return True if the sequence reaches 1; return False if it repeats without reaching 1.
target_time_complexity: O(log n) to process the initial digits, then bounded-state cycle work for 32-bit inputs
hints: The next number is deterministic, so revisiting a number means the future will repeat.
Use cycle detection: one pointer advances once and the other twice through the digit-square transformation.
Stop when the fast pointer reaches 1 or the pointers meet; only reaching 1 is happy.
Arithmetic digit extraction and two pointers avoid storing the full history; a visited set is another valid approach.
editorial: The digit-square transformation quickly enters a bounded set of small numbers. Floyd's slow/fast pointers detect a repeated state without a history set. Reaching 1 is the successful fixed point; a meeting elsewhere is a nonhappy cycle. The independent oracle instead converts numbers to strings, squares each digit, and retains every visited value in a set.

tests.explanation: The sequence is 19→82→68→100→1, so 19 is happy even though its first transformation is not 1.
The sequence eventually repeats the cycle 4→16→37→58→89→145→42→20→4 and never reaches 1.
